extracted.intended_audience: Members of Parliament, policy-makers, journalists, and the interested public following the Hutton report and BBC governance
extracted.subtask_description: Transcript of House of Lords speeches debating the Hutton report, the BBC's handling of the Gilligan/David Kelly affair, the meaning of 'sexing-up' and the proper remit and conduct of subsequent inquiries. Includes critiques of intelligence handling, editorial standards, and inquiry terms of reference.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of 'sexed-up' (Hutton report)
rubrics_metrics.description: The term 'sexed-up' is a slang expression, the meaning of which lacks clarity in the context of the discussion of the dossier. It is capable of two different meanings. It could mean that the dossier was embellished with items of intelligence known or believed to be false or unreliable to make the case against Saddam Hussein stronger. ... It could mean that whilst the intelligence contained in the dossier was believed to be reliable, the dossier was drafted in such a way as to make the case against Saddam Hussein as strong as the intelligence contained in it permitted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Two distinct senses must be kept separate when assessing allegations: (1) insertion/presentation of intelligence known or believed to be false (an 'unfounded' allegation according to Hutton in the Gilligan broadcast context), and (2) drafting to make the case stronger within the bounds of available intelligence (a practice critics wish to examine). The distinction affects culpability and findings.

rubrics_metrics.name: BBC core values: impartiality, accuracy and trust
rubrics_metrics.description: Impartiality, accuracy and trust have always been core BBC values designed to serve the public.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These values should guide editorial decisions and organisational leadership. Maintaining them includes robust editorial frameworks that allow for brave, independent and rigorous journalism while safeguarding objectivity when reporting sensitive matters such as self-review. The board and executives should protect editorial independence while ensuring adherence to these values.

rubrics_metrics.name: Investigate and correct editorial mistakes
rubrics_metrics.description: The BBC must undertake a review of the lessons it must learn from the past few months, including how the corporation investigates and corrects editorial mistakes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Appropriate responses include prompt corrections, proportionate apologies, transparent internal review, accountability of leadership (resignation where appropriate), and mechanisms to avoid disproportionate punishment relative to other wrongdoers. Leadership should enable internal lessons-learning without unjustified external interference.

rubrics_metrics.name: JIC assessment process and handling of dissent
rubrics_metrics.description: The JIC process is one where assessments are thrashed out round a table, usually at ad hoc current intelligence groups, and then, once an assessment has emerged, it is up to every participating service to go back to its headquarters and brief its head. If anyone is not happy about the assessment then they brief in writing accordingly and it is up to the top person to decide on the merits or otherwise of the case. It is for that person to speak for the service or organisation at the JIC.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proper process requires documented dissent and clear responsibility for speaking for each service. Awareness of the distinction between intelligence officers and other users of intelligence (e.g., DIS officers) is important when evaluating the provenance and authority of assessments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Risk of political (subconscious) influence on intelligence
rubrics_metrics.description: The possibility cannot be ruled out that John Scarlett and other members of the JIC may have been subconsciously influenced by knowing that the PM wanted to have a dossier worded as strongly as possible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing intelligence products, reviewers should consider whether political preferences or expectations (conscious or subconscious) affected drafting. Robust safeguards and transparency (e.g., recorded drafting suggestions, e-mails) help determine whether wording reflected available intelligence or political shaping.

rubrics_metrics.name: Remit of inquiries: hold government to account and restore public confidence
rubrics_metrics.description: One sets up committees of inquiry for a number of purposes. The first is to hold a government to account and the second, but equally important, is to attempt to re-establish public confidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Terms of reference should be broad enough to address these aims. Overly narrow terms invite public scepticism and accusations of whitewash. Historical examples (e.g., broader inquiries examining 'origins, inception and conduct') show broader remits better serve public reassurance and accountability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarity and appropriateness of terms of reference and process
rubrics_metrics.description: The terms of reference are obviously most important. Confusion about appointments (e.g., unexpected Privy Counsellors) and rushed set-up undermines confidence in the inquiry process.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Inquiries should have clearly defined, agreed terms of reference and a well-planned appointment/process timeline (advertisement, shortlist, final choice) to avoid perceptions of mishandling or political manipulation. Participation agreements between parties should be honoured or clearly renegotiated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Handling and naming of sources
rubrics_metrics.description: With hindsight his name should have been concealed or it should have been announced having given Dr Kelly clear warning of that so that arrangements could be made for him. The idea of a 'Twenty Questions' exercise to see whether the media guessed the right name was most regrettable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Best practice: protect anonymity of sources unless explicit, informed consent to identification is obtained; if naming is necessary, provide prior warning and safeguards. Public or careless naming without warning is unethical and can have serious consequences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Journalistic standards: report, don't create news; verify sources
rubrics_metrics.description: The 'Today' programme has become one of extraordinary political significance. It is a battleground of political ideas... There were elements of tabloid and Sunday journalism in which it appeared to be avoiding contacting people who might deny its story. Kevin Marsh said the BBC had recruited Mr Gilligan so that he might get up the nose of the Government.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Journalists should: (a) verify the nature of a source (distinguish 'user of intelligence' from 'intelligence source'), (b) contact those who might deny the story to allow balance and correction, (c) avoid adopting tabloid techniques that create rather than report news, and (d) avoid editorial commissioning aimed primarily at antagonising subjects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Presentation of government intelligence and the case for action
rubrics_metrics.description: The charge is that the Government stretched the evidence, that it massaged the evidence. The Prime Minister had to rest the case for war far more on weapons of mass destruction than his American allies did in order to persuade a more sceptical British Parliament and public.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When government presents intelligence to justify major actions (e.g., military intervention), it must avoid overstating uncertain evidence, present the range and limits of intelligence clearly, and ensure claims do not exceed what the intelligence supports. Failure to do so raises questions about motivations and undermines public trust.
